articles.title: Your DNS TTL is why the outage lasted 2 hours: set it before you need it
articles.excerpt: The server died at 14:02. A new one was up at 14:20, and the A record was updated at 14:21. Half the users were still hitting the dead IP at 16:00. The fix took a minute. The TTL was 86400. DNS change…
articles.body: The server died at 14:02. A new one was up at 14:20, and the A record was updated at 14:21. Half the users were still hitting the dead IP at 16:00. The fix took a minute. The TTL was 86400. DNS changes don't "propagate". Resolvers cache your old answer for as long as you told them they could, and you told them a day. TL;DR TTL is a promise: "you may cache this answer for N seconds". Resolvers keep that promise even when you change your mind. Lowering a TTL only helps after the old TTL has expired. Lower it at least one old-TTL ahead of any planned change. 300 seconds is a sane default for records you might need to move. 3600+ is fine for records that never change. My opinion: "DNS propagation takes 24 to 48 hours" is mostly a myth caused by long TTLs people set themselves.

articles.title: Ping is not an uptime check: 5 ways ICMP lies about whether your site is up
articles.excerpt: The monitor said the server was up: 0% packet loss, 12 ms round trip. The site had been returning 502 Bad Gateway for forty minutes. Nobody got paged, because the uptime check was a ping. The opposite…
articles.body: The monitor said the server was up: 0% packet loss, 12 ms round trip. The site had been returning 502 Bad Gateway for forty minutes. Nobody got paged, because the uptime check was a ping. The opposite happens too. A team moves behind a cloud firewall, ping starts timing out, and the pager goes off at 3 AM for a site that is serving traffic perfectly well. TL;DR Ping tests whether a host answers ICMP echo. Users don't use ICMP. They use DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP. Ping can be green during a full outage and red during perfect health. For uptime, check an HTTP request to a real page, with a timeout and a content check. My opinion: ping-based uptime monitoring for websites should be retired. Use it only as a diagnostic.

articles.title: Your health check returns 200 while users get errors: 7 health check mistakes
articles.excerpt: The dashboard was green. The load balancer was happy. Every /health probe returned 200 OK in 4 ms. Meanwhile, every checkout request was failing because the database connection pool was exhausted, and…
articles.body: The dashboard was green. The load balancer was happy. Every /health probe returned 200 OK in 4 ms. Meanwhile, every checkout request was failing because the database connection pool was exhausted, and nobody found out until support tickets started piling up. If that sounds familiar, the health check wasn't broken. It was answering a different question than the one you cared about. TL;DR A health check that only proves the process is alive will stay green through most real outages. Split it in two: a cheap liveness check and a readiness check that touches real dependencies with tight timeouts. Monitor from the outside on a real user path too. Your own /health can't see DNS, TLS or CDN problems. My opinion: a single /health endpoint used for everything is a design smell.

articles.title: Golden-File Tests for a Score Calculator: Check Every Row Against the Published Table
articles.excerpt: If you build a calculator that turns a raw result into points, the scoring table is the product. A bug in the arithmetic is easy to spot. A single wrong row in a 100-line table is not, and users will…
articles.body: If you build a calculator that turns a raw result into points, the scoring table is the product. A bug in the arithmetic is easy to spot. A single wrong row in a 100-line table is not, and users will trust it anyway. This post shows a small way to protect a lookup-table calculator: keep the table as data, keep a second copy of the source numbers as a "golden file," and test every row automatically. The numbers in the examples below are made up for illustration. When you build one for a real standard, copy the values from the governing document and cite it on the page. Step 1: keep the table as data, not code Hard-coding thresholds inside if statements makes them impossible to review.

articles.body: PART 1. WHAT YOU KNOW ABOUT THRIVE (use this in your answers) Company is 10+ years old, everything runs on AWS. Core app is PHP, mostly APIs for mobile apps, plus smaller APIs. They moved from a Puppet-based system to Kubernetes on EKS. CI is GitHub Actions, CD is Argo CD. Still have legacy systems in different AWS accounts. They want to move them into the main prod account (caches, ALBs, services). Biggest priorities: cost, legacy migration, Kubernetes work. Most incidents are app-related: DB slowness or cache issues make PHP-FPM workers fill up, Nginx upstream queues grow, error rate goes up. One past infra issue: CPU steal on Kubernetes nodes. They care about early signals, SLOs, and error rate. They are starting to use AI for monitoring.

Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis. articles.title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
articles.excerpt: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automa…
articles.body: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired. Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed.
